steps.consequence: That lipid becomes a docking site. Whatever can read PIP3 will now be pulled to the membrane.
steps.certainty: Mechanistically secure and drawn as a long dash precisely because it is compressed. Cited evidence is cell-line work, so human relevance is plausible, not established.
steps.matters: The cell's answer to 'am I allowed to grow?' does not arrive as a molecule entering the cytosol. It arrives as a change in membrane chemistry. That is why this arm is reversed by a phosphatase rather than switched off by degradation.

steps.what: PIP3 recruits Akt to the membrane — and recruitment is not activation.
steps.why: Akt has a domain that binds PIP3. Arriving at the membrane puts it where two kinases can reach it, but arriving is not the same as being switched on: PDK1 must phosphorylate T308 and mTORC2 must phosphorylate S473.
steps.changed: Akt's location changes. Its activity changes only once the two phosphorylations happen.
steps.consequence: Full growth-factor signalling therefore depends on mTORC2 being functional — which is why mTOR sits on both sides of this pathway.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, well replicated, cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: The same distinction as in the nutrient arm, appearing again: getting a protein to a place is a different act from switching it on. A diagram with one arrow from PI3K to Akt hides three events and one dependency on the other mTOR complex.

steps.what: Akt phosphorylates the TSC complex and takes the brake off.
steps.why: TSC1/TSC2 is the pathway's master brake. Akt phosphorylation inhibits it — partly by changing its activity, substantially by moving it away from where its target sits.
steps.changed: The brake stops being applied. Nothing has been pushed yet; something has stopped being held back.
steps.consequence: Whatever the brake was suppressing is now free to act. That target is Rheb.
steps.certainty: This is one of the two papers the route's Journey header names as its breakthrough (INO2002). High mechanistic confidence; cell-line evidence, so human relevance plausible — though TSC loss in people is the one place this pathway's causality is established.
steps.matters: Double-negative logic again, exactly as in the nutrient arm. Growth signals in this pathway overwhelmingly work by removing inhibition rather than adding stimulation. Once you see that pattern you stop being surprised by it.

steps.what: Released from Akt's inhibition, TSC would switch Rheb off — so inhibiting TSC leaves Rheb loaded.
steps.why: TSC2 is a GAP: it forces Rheb to hydrolyse GTP to GDP. With TSC inhibited, Rheb accumulates in its GTP state.
steps.changed: Rheb flips from GDP-loaded to GTP-loaded. This is the moment the growth-factor signal becomes a switch position.
steps.consequence: GTP-Rheb can now do the one thing in this pathway that genuinely activates mTORC1.
steps.certainty: The second breakthrough paper (INOK2003), with GAR2003 independently. High mechanistic confidence; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: Note how far the signal has travelled and how little has been 'activated': a hormone bound a receptor, a lipid was made, a kinase was recruited, a brake was released, and a GTPase changed nucleotide. Four negations and a nucleotide swap. That is what a signalling pathway actually is.

steps.what: GTP-Rheb binds mTORC1 and switches the kinase on.
steps.why: Rheb realigns the mTOR active site into a catalytically competent conformation. This is an allosteric activation — structurally different from everything upstream.
steps.changed: mTORC1 becomes an active kinase. Now, and only now, its substrates start getting phosphorylated.
steps.consequence: The cell begins to build. And because this step happens at the lysosome, it can only happen if the nutrient arm has already delivered mTORC1 there.
steps.certainty: Structurally resolved, high mechanistic confidence, cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: This is the convergence point of the whole map. The nutrient arm answers 'are the parts available' by controlling location; this arm answers 'am I allowed' by controlling Rheb. Both must be satisfied at the same membrane at the same time — and this step is where the AND gate is evaluated.

steps.what: Active mTORC1 phosphorylates S6K1.
steps.why: S6K1 carries a TOS motif recognised by Raptor, which presents it to the kinase. T389 phosphorylation activates it.
steps.changed: S6K1 becomes an active kinase with its own substrates.
steps.consequence: Two things follow, and they point in opposite directions. S6K1 promotes translation — and it also starts dismantling the signal that created it.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, replicated, and this is the classical rapamycin-sensitive readout. Cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: S6K1's rapamycin sensitivity is why it became the field's default assay for 'mTORC1 activity' — and why the field systematically overestimated how completely rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 for years. The convenience of a readout shaped what people believed.

steps.what: S6K1 phosphorylates IRS-1 and marks it for destruction.
steps.why: Serine phosphorylation of IRS-1 creates a degradation signal. The adaptor that connected the receptor to PI3K is removed.
steps.changed: IRS-1 protein levels fall. The input arm of this very route is dismantled.
steps.consequence: PI3K recruitment drops, Akt activity falls, and the growth signal decays — even though the hormone is still present.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, multiple supporting studies. Cell-line evidence, so human relevance graded plausible, though the clinical consequence is well documented.
steps.matters: This is negative feedback, and it is the most clinically consequential loop in the pathway. Block mTORC1 with a rapalog and you also block this loop — so IRS-1 survives, PI3K/Akt reactivate, and the tumour you were treating gets a growth signal back. Half the reason rapalog monotherapy underperforms is visible in this single arrow.

steps.what: IRS-1 recruits PI3K — closing the loop back to step one.
steps.why: IRS-1 is the scaffold that brings PI3K to the activated receptor. Its abundance sets how much signal gets through.
steps.changed: The route returns to where it started. This is not a chain; it is a cycle with a set point.
steps.consequence: The steady state of growth-factor signalling is determined by the balance between the forward arm and this feedback arm — not by the hormone concentration alone.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: The question was how a cell learns it is allowed to grow. The answer turns out to be that it never simply learns — it continuously negotiates. The pathway measures its own output and turns its own input down. Any drug that interrupts the loop changes the negotiation, which is why mTOR inhibitors have effects nobody predicted from the linear diagram.

routes.name: Why doesn't rapamycin switch mTOR off completely?

journey.title: Why doesn't rapamycin switch mTOR off completely?
journey.question: Rapamycin was the drug that discovered this pathway, and for a decade it was treated as *the* mTOR inhibitor. But cells treated with rapamycin keep doing some of the things mTORC1 drives. Why does a drug that clearly hits mTOR fail to stop all of its outputs?

breakthrough.why: Built an ATP-competitive inhibitor and used it as a ruler. Comparing it against rapamycin exposed a whole class of rapamycin-RESISTANT mTORC1 outputs — most importantly 4E-BP1 phosphorylation, which rapamycin barely touches while collapsing S6K1. That single comparison explained a decade of confusing results and launched the second-generation inhibitor programme that reached trials by 2025.

journey.evidence: Pharmacological comparison plus biochemistry in cell lines, with the structural basis (FKBP12–rapamycin occluding the substrate channel rather than the active site) resolved separately. The clinical consequence is supported by trial evidence; the mechanism is not human data.
journey.unknowns: Whether chronic rapamycin genuinely disrupts mTORC2 is contested and appears to be cell-type and duration dependent. How much the 4E-BP escape matters in any particular tumour is unresolved, which is precisely the question bi-steric inhibitors are being trialled to answer.

routes.summary: One drug, two complexes, and a time axis. Most confusion about rapamycin comes from ignoring the third of those.
routes.story: The drug is a two-part molecule: rapamycin alone does nothing, rapamycin+FKBP12 blocks mTORC1 — but only partially, which is why 4E-BP1 stays half-phosphorylated. The dashed arrow to mTORC2 is the one everyone gets wrong: it does not exist acutely, only after days of exposure. That single time-dependence separates the benefit from the side effect.

steps.what: Rapamycin binds FKBP12 — and on its own, does nothing to mTOR.
steps.why: Rapamycin is not an mTOR inhibitor in the way that word is normally used. It has essentially no activity against mTOR by itself. It first binds a small abundant prolyl isomerase, FKBP12, and the drug-protein pair becomes the actual inhibitor.
steps.changed: A new molecular surface exists that did not exist before: the FKBP12–rapamycin composite. Neither half has that surface alone.
steps.consequence: Because the inhibitor is a complex, how much inhibition a cell experiences depends on how much FKBP12 that cell expresses — not only on drug concentration.
steps.certainty: Structurally resolved and mechanistically secure. Cited evidence is cell-line and structural work, so human relevance is graded plausible rather than established.
steps.matters: This is the first clue that rapamycin will behave oddly. A drug that must borrow a host protein to work is a drug whose potency varies with the host. It also explains why FKBP12 expression is a determinant of rapalog sensitivity — a fact with no analogue in ordinary ATP-competitive inhibitors.

steps.what: The complex binds the FRB domain and partially blocks the substrate channel.
steps.why: It does not enter the active site. It docks on a domain adjacent to it and gets in the way of substrates arriving. That is a different kind of inhibition from occupying the catalytic pocket — it is steric obstruction, and obstruction can be partial.
steps.changed: mTORC1 remains a catalytically intact kinase. What changes is which substrates can still reach it.
steps.consequence: Substrates that need deep, sustained access lose out. Substrates that need less access carry on. The pathway does not switch off — it becomes selectively deaf.
steps.certainty: Structurally resolved, high mechanistic confidence. The clinical consequences are supported by trial evidence; this mechanism is not human data.
steps.matters: Here is the answer to the route's question, and almost the whole field missed it for a decade. Because rapamycin obstructs rather than occupies, S6K1 phosphorylation collapses while 4E-BP1 phosphorylation largely survives. Every experiment that used S6K1 as 'the mTORC1 readout' therefore over-reported how much rapamycin inhibits mTORC1.

steps.what: One output rapamycin does release: mTORC1 stops holding ULK1 down.
steps.why: mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1 on S757, which blocks ULK1 from being activated by AMPK. Inhibit mTORC1 and that block lifts.
steps.changed: ULK1 becomes available to AMPK. Autophagy initiation is no longer suppressed.
steps.consequence: The cell starts recycling. This is the arm of rapamycin's action that behaves the way people expect a clean inhibitor to behave.
steps.certainty: Direct biochemistry, replicated across labs; mechanistic confidence high, evidence from mammalian cells.
steps.matters: Notice the asymmetry this creates. Rapamycin turns autophagy on fairly reliably while only partly turning protein synthesis off. It is not a dimmer switch on 'mTORC1 activity' — it reshapes the output profile. That asymmetry is why rapamycin can extend lifespan in mice while being a mediocre anti-proliferative in many tumours.

steps.what: ULK1 initiates autophagy.
steps.why: Freed and phosphorylated by AMPK, ULK1 nucleates the machinery that builds an autophagosome.
steps.changed: Bulk degradative recycling begins: damaged proteins and organelles are captured and delivered to lysosomes.
steps.consequence: The cell buys time and materials. Most of the healthspan claims made for rapamycin route through this step.
steps.certainty: Mechanistically solid. But autophagic FLUX is genuinely hard to measure in tissue rather than cells, so quantitative in vivo claims about how much autophagy a given rapamycin dose produces are weaker than they sound.
steps.matters: This is where the rapamycin story usually stops being told carefully. 'Rapamycin induces autophagy therefore it extends lifespan' skips the part where nobody has cleanly shown autophagy is the required mediator in a mammal.

steps.what: Given long enough, rapamycin also disturbs mTORC2 — sometimes.
steps.why: Chronic exposure can interfere with mTORC2 assembly in some cell types. This is not the acute, direct inhibition seen with mTORC1; it is a slower, indirect effect on complex integrity.
steps.changed: In susceptible cells, mTORC2 output falls. In others, it does not.
steps.consequence: The clean textbook statement 'rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 but not mTORC2' is true acutely and unreliable chronically — which matters enormously, because patients take rapalogs chronically.
steps.certainty: Contested, low mechanistic confidence, a single supporting study in this corpus. Cell type and duration both change the answer. This is drawn as a dashed line with an amber halo for exactly that reason.
steps.matters: A route that taught only the tidy version would be teaching a fact with a hidden expiry date. The honest position is that acute and chronic rapamycin are different drugs pharmacologically, and most of what people 'know' about rapamycin comes from acute experiments.

steps.what: Losing mTORC2 is one route to insulin resistance.
steps.why: mTORC2 phosphorylates Akt on S473. Reduce that and insulin signalling degrades, which in mice produces measurable glucose intolerance.
steps.changed: Whole-body glucose handling worsens — an organism-level consequence, not a cellular one.
steps.consequence: This is the leading mechanistic explanation for the dysglycaemia seen in patients on rapalogs.
steps.certainty: Mouse data, tier C, medium mechanistic confidence. In humans the relative contributions of mTORC2 loss, S6K1–IRS-1 feedback and direct beta-cell effects are unresolved — so attributing the clinical side effect to this one mechanism overstates what is known.
steps.matters: The most common serious side effect of the drug may be caused by the arm the textbook says the drug does not hit. If chronic rapamycin does reach mTORC2, then the 'selective mTORC1 inhibitor' framing is not just imprecise, it is clinically misleading.

steps.what: And still, rapamycin extends lifespan in mice.
steps.why: Reproducibly, across genetically heterogeneous strains, at multiple independent sites, including when started late in life.
steps.changed: Median and maximum lifespan increase. This is one of the most robust pharmacological longevity results in mammals.
steps.consequence: Everything upstream in this route — partial inhibition, asymmetric outputs, possible mTORC2 disruption, insulin resistance — is the mechanism this outcome sits on. The outcome is solid; the causal chain is not.
steps.certainty: Strong for mice: replicated, multi-site, tier C. For humans: there is no lifespan data of any kind. Human relevance is graded untested, and that grade is not pessimism, it is arithmetic.
steps.matters: The question this route asked was why rapamycin does not switch mTOR off completely. The answer may be why it works at all. A complete mTOR shutdown is lethal; partial, asymmetric inhibition that suppresses growth signalling while permitting recycling may be exactly the therapeutic window — achieved by accident, through a drug that obstructs rather than occupies.

routes.name: What does a cell actually do when mTORC1 fires?

journey.title: What does a cell actually do when mTORC1 fires?
journey.question: 'Promotes growth' is not a mechanism. If mTORC1 switching on has consequences, those consequences are specific molecules being made and specific processes being stopped. Which ones — and does mTORC1 turn everything up equally?

breakthrough.why: Answered the second half, which almost everyone had assumed away. Ribosome profiling showed mTORC1 does not raise translation uniformly — it selectively promotes a specific class of transcripts. 'mTORC1 increases protein synthesis' turned out to be a summary that hides the actual biology, which is transcript choice.

journey.evidence: Ribosome profiling and biochemistry in cancer cell lines for the selectivity; genetic knockouts in mice for the phenotypic arms (muscle, mitochondria, lipid). The output-to-phenotype steps are the weakest links in the route, and they are graded accordingly.
journey.unknowns: How much of the mTOR-responsive phosphoproteome is functionally relevant rather than incidental. Which outputs matter for which phenotype — the map draws mTORC1 to muscle growth and to longevity, but these are not the same kind of claim and the second has no human evidence at all.

routes.summary: Where the signalling stops being signalling. Eight branches leave mTORC1, and they do not share a fate: rapamycin blocks some completely, others barely at all.
routes.story: Follow the spine: mTORC1 releases 4E-BP1, 4E-BP1 lets go of eIF4E, translation runs, muscle is built. Then look at what does not follow that line. Rapamycin blocks S6K1 almost completely but 4E-BP1 only partly - which is why 'mTORC1 activity' measured as p-S6K can look abolished while half the real output carries on. And the two lifespan arrows point in opposite directions: losing S6K1 extends life, keeping 4E-BP active extends life. One node is not the pathway.

steps.what: mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP1 and releases a brake on translation.
steps.why: 4E-BP1 sits on eIF4E and prevents it from starting translation. Multi-site phosphorylation by mTORC1 makes 4E-BP1 let go.
steps.changed: eIF4E becomes available. Note the direction: a phosphate was ADDED, and the effect is to STOP an inhibitor — phosphorylation is a mechanism, not a sign.
steps.consequence: Cap-dependent translation initiation can begin.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, well replicated; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: This one substrate carries more consequence than any other in the pathway, because it is only PARTLY rapamycin-sensitive. That single property explains the rapalog/Torin discrepancy and motivated the entire second-generation inhibitor programme.

steps.what: Free of 4E-BP1, eIF4E can bind eIF4G.
steps.why: 4E-BP1 and eIF4G compete for the same surface on eIF4E. Removing one lets the other bind — competitive inhibition, not enzymatic.
steps.changed: The initiation complex can assemble on capped mRNA.
steps.consequence: Ribosomes begin loading. The cell starts making protein.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, structurally understood; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: Competition is a distinct mechanism from catalysis, and it behaves differently: it is concentration-sensitive and instantly reversible. That is why 4E-BP:eIF4E stoichiometry matters as much as mTORC1 activity, and why tissues with different 4E-BP levels respond differently to the same drug.

steps.what: Translation increases — but not uniformly.
steps.why: Ribosome profiling showed mTORC1 does not raise all translation equally. It selectively promotes a specific class of transcripts.
steps.changed: The composition of what the cell is making changes, not just the amount.
steps.consequence: Which proteins increase determines which phenotype follows — and those transcripts are enriched for growth and invasion programmes.
steps.certainty: This is the route's breakthrough paper (HSI2012). High mechanistic confidence; cancer cell lines, so human relevance plausible.
steps.matters: 'mTORC1 increases protein synthesis' is the summary that hides the actual biology. The regulated variable is transcript CHOICE. Anyone reasoning about mTOR from the summary will predict the wrong consequences, because a uniform increase and a selective one have different phenotypes.

steps.what: In muscle, that translation supports hypertrophy.
steps.why: Load-driven growth requires mTORC1: Raptor-null muscle is dystrophic, and rapamycin blocks overload-induced hypertrophy.
steps.changed: Muscle fibres grow — over days, not minutes.
steps.consequence: This is one of the few places where the pathway's output has been tested in people.
steps.certainty: The strongest human evidence in this route: DRU2009 is a tier-B human interventional study showing rapamycin blocks the contraction-induced increase in muscle protein synthesis. Human relevance established, not merely plausible.
steps.matters: Worth pausing on, because it is rare. Most of this map is graded human-relevance plausible on cell-line evidence. Here a human intervention closes the loop. It also carries a caveat: mTORC1 activation is NECESSARY for healthy hypertrophy but not sufficient — constitutive activation alone does not build good muscle.

steps.what: At the same time, mTORC1 is holding recycling down.
steps.why: Phosphorylation of ULK1 on S757 blocks the AMPK–ULK1 interaction, preventing autophagy initiation.
steps.changed: Autophagy is suppressed while building proceeds.
steps.consequence: The two arms are reciprocal by design: the cell does not build and demolish simultaneously.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, replicated; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: This is the answer to what mTORC1 firing actually DOES, stated properly: it is not one action but a coordinated switch between two mutually exclusive programmes. Any account that lists only the build side has described half a switch.

steps.what: Release mTORC1 and autophagy resumes.
steps.why: Unblocked ULK1 nucleates autophagosome formation, and TFEB — released from mTORC1 phosphorylation — transcribes the genes to sustain it.
steps.changed: The cell shifts from building to recycling, at both the initiation and the transcriptional level.
steps.consequence: Materials are regenerated. Over longer timescales this arm is where most healthspan claims for mTOR inhibition are made.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence for initiation. Autophagic flux in tissue is genuinely hard to measure, so in vivo quantitative claims are weaker than the mechanism.
steps.matters: Two independent control points — a kinase switch in minutes and a transcriptional programme in hours — on the same process. That is how the pathway gets both a fast response and a sustained one out of a single input.

steps.what: And deleting one output extends lifespan — in female mice.
steps.why: S6K1-null mice live longer and resist age-related pathology, which is the cleanest genetic evidence that a specific mTORC1 output influences lifespan.
steps.changed: Median lifespan increases, along with metabolic protection.
steps.consequence: It suggests the longevity effect of mTOR inhibition can be traced to particular outputs rather than to 'less mTOR' in general.
steps.certainty: Tier C mouse genetics, medium mechanistic confidence, human relevance untested. And the effect is SEX-SPECIFIC — reported in females — a qualification routinely dropped when this result is cited.
steps.matters: The route asked what a cell does when mTORC1 fires. The honest ending is that we can trace it from a kinase to a phosphosite to a translational programme to a phenotype in one sex of one species — and that no step of that chain has been demonstrated in a human. The map is strongest at the top and weakest exactly where people most want to use it.

routes.name: How does a cell decide it cannot afford to grow?

journey.title: How does a cell decide it cannot afford to grow?
journey.question: Building is expensive. A cell that starts a growth programme it cannot fuel will damage itself. So there must be a way for energy status to override a growth instruction that has already been given — and it has to work even when the usual brake is broken.

breakthrough.why: Found the arm nobody expected: AMPK phosphorylates Raptor directly, inhibiting mTORC1 without going through the TSC complex at all. That explained why TSC2-null cells still shut down under energy stress, and it established that this pathway has redundant brakes rather than one master switch.

journey.evidence: Direct biochemistry and genetic epistasis in mammalian cells, with the two AMPK arms separable using TSC-null lines. LKB1 dependence means cell lines lacking LKB1 cannot mount the response at all — a boundary condition that invalidates naive comparison across cell types.
journey.unknowns: The relative weight of the TSC2 arm versus the Raptor arm in intact tissue is not resolved, and it is cell-type dependent. The metformin route is genuinely contested: several mechanisms are proposed, and the concentrations used in vitro often exceed what clinical dosing achieves.

routes.summary: The third input. Nutrients say what is available and growth factors say whether to bother; stress overrides both.
routes.story: Three different stresses, three different speeds. AMPK reads falling ATP in seconds. REDD1 needs low oxygen to switch on a gene, so it is minutes. The integrated stress response is slower still. All three converge on the same two brakes - and notice AMPK does not only lift the brake on autophagy, it pushes ULK1 directly. That is the pathway doing arithmetic rather than relaying. One caveat on the left-hand corner: metformin is drawn into AMPK because that is the route it is usually credited to, but the dashed arrow running past AMPK straight to mTORC1 is real - metformin still works in AMPK-null and LKB1-null tissue. How the two routes divide the labour in people is unresolved.

steps.what: Falling energy charge activates AMPK directly.
steps.why: AMP and ADP bind the AMPK gamma subunit, which both activates the kinase allosterically and protects its activating phosphorylation from being removed. The cell is not reading 'low ATP' — it is reading the RATIO.
steps.changed: AMPK becomes active within seconds of the energy charge dropping.
steps.consequence: A kinase is now running whose entire job is to stop expensive processes and start cheap ones.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, well replicated; cell-line evidence, so human relevance plausible.
steps.matters: Reading a ratio rather than an absolute is what makes this a sensor rather than a thermometer. A cell with genuinely low but stable ATP is not in trouble; a cell whose ATP is falling is. The ratio distinguishes them.

steps.what: AMPK phosphorylates and activates the TSC complex.
steps.why: Where Akt phosphorylation inhibited TSC, AMPK phosphorylation at different sites activates it. The same brake, driven in the opposite direction by a different kinase.
steps.changed: TSC GAP activity rises. Rheb starts being switched off.
steps.consequence: The growth-factor signal is overridden. A cell that was told to grow can now refuse.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, though on a single tier-D study in this corpus — the validator flags it, and it is fair to note that the corpus here is thinner than the literature.
steps.matters: Two opposing inputs converge on one protein, and TSC becomes the place where 'permitted' and 'affordable' are reconciled. Integration in this pathway is not a special mechanism; it is several kinases writing to the same substrate.

steps.what: Activated TSC drives Rheb back to its GDP state.
steps.why: Same GAP reaction as in the growth-factor route, running the other way because TSC is now active rather than inhibited.
steps.changed: GTP-Rheb falls. The mTORC1 on-switch is being withdrawn.
steps.consequence: mTORC1 activity declines even if nutrients are plentiful and hormones are still signalling.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: Energy status wins. Of the four inputs on the overview diagram, this is the one that can veto the others — which makes biological sense, because a cell that builds without fuel destroys itself.

steps.what: With Rheb off, mTORC1 goes quiet.
steps.why: No GTP-Rheb, no allosteric activation, no active kinase — regardless of where mTORC1 is sitting.
steps.changed: mTORC1 stops phosphorylating its substrates. Building stops.
steps.consequence: But stopping growth is only half of what an energy-starved cell needs. It also needs to generate resources.
steps.certainty: Structurally resolved; high mechanistic confidence.
steps.matters: This is the same step the growth-factor route ended on, reached from the opposite direction. Seeing one node arrived at by two different arms is how the map teaches convergence — and why 'mTORC1 activity' is never explained by a single upstream signal.

steps.what: In parallel, AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 and switches recycling on.
steps.why: AMPK acts on ULK1 directly, at sites distinct from the inhibitory site mTORC1 uses. And with mTORC1 now quiet, the mTORC1 block on ULK1 has lifted too.
steps.changed: Autophagy initiation is both released and actively driven — two independent pushes in the same direction.
steps.consequence: The cell starts digesting its own components to regenerate substrates.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, direct biochemistry, replicated.
steps.matters: This is the elegant part of energy sensing. One kinase performs both halves of the switch: it stops the expensive programme and starts the recovery programme, simultaneously, without needing a second sensor. Note also that ULK1 phosphorylates AMPK back — so this is a loop with a set point, not a one-way command.

steps.what: Selectively, damaged mitochondria are recycled.
steps.why: AMPK promotes mitophagy, the targeted autophagy of mitochondria — which is both a quality-control mechanism and a way to reclaim material.
steps.changed: Dysfunctional mitochondria are cleared rather than left to leak.
steps.consequence: Over longer timescales this shapes mitochondrial quality, and it is one of the arms through which energy stress is proposed to influence ageing.
steps.certainty: Medium mechanistic confidence, indirect, and measured largely with reporter mice — so quantitative claims are model-bound. Mouse evidence, human relevance plausible at best.
steps.matters: The route began with a question about affordability and ends with quality control. That is not a digression: a cell short of energy is usually a cell with failing mitochondria, so the same signal that stops growth is the right signal to trigger repair of the cause. Energy sensing is not a thermostat — it is a diagnostic.

routes.name: Why does one kinase need two complexes?

journey.title: Why does one kinase need two complexes?
journey.question: mTOR is a single protein, yet it does two jobs that respond to different signals, sit in different places, and have different drug sensitivities. Why did evolution not simply use two kinases — and how do you study one of two jobs when your only tool inhibits the other?

breakthrough.why: Identified Rictor and, with it, a second mTOR complex that is raptor-independent and — decisively — rapamycin-insensitive. That last property is what made mTORC2 studiable at all: it gave the field a way to separate the two jobs experimentally, using the very drug that had previously hidden one of them.

journey.evidence: Biochemistry and complex purification in mammalian cells, then genetic dissection in knockout mice (Rictor and mLST8 loss abolishes signalling to Akt and PKCα while sparing S6K1). The mouse genetics is the strongest evidence in this route.
journey.unknowns: Whether prolonged rapamycin disrupts mTORC2 assembly is contested. The mTORC2-to-insulin-resistance link rests on mouse data, and in humans the relative contributions of mTORC2 loss, S6K1–IRS-1 feedback and direct β-cell effects are unresolved.

routes.summary: The same kinase, a different set of partners, and almost none of the same drugs. Half the mTOR story, usually told as a footnote to rapamycin's side effects.
routes.story: mLST8 is the clean argument that these really are two machines: delete it and mTORC2 dies while mTORC1 carries on. Everything below mTORC2 was discovered because rapamycin failed to block it - the actin cytoskeleton first. And the dashed arrow from rapamycin is the whole clinical problem in one line: absent acutely, present after days.

steps.what: Rictor binds mTOR and defines a second complex.
steps.why: The same catalytic subunit, a different partner. Rictor takes the place Raptor occupies in mTORC1, and the resulting complex has different substrates, a different location and — decisively — different drug sensitivity.
steps.changed: There are now two mTOR complexes in the cell, not one kinase with two moods.
steps.consequence: Because Rictor confers rapamycin insensitivity, this complex was invisible for a decade to anyone using rapamycin as their probe.
steps.certainty: This is the route's breakthrough paper (SAR2004). High mechanistic confidence, biochemistry and complex purification in mammalian cells.
steps.matters: The answer to the route's question starts here. Evolution did not need two kinases because the catalytic domain is not what specifies a signalling job — the partner is. Substrate choice, location and regulation all come from the accessory subunit, so one kinase gene can serve two pathways.

steps.what: SIN1 joins, and brings a growth-factor antenna with it.
steps.why: SIN1 is required for complex integrity and for Akt S473 kinase activity. Its PH domain inhibits mTORC2 until PIP3 relieves that inhibition.
steps.changed: mTORC2 becomes assembled, competent, and responsive to membrane lipid state.
steps.consequence: The complex now has a way to know whether growth factors are present — through the same PIP3 signal Akt uses.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, multiple studies including structural work.
steps.matters: A subunit doubling as a sensor is an economical piece of design: the same lipid that recruits the substrate also licenses the kinase. It also means PI3K sits upstream of both arms, which is why PI3K inhibition has broader consequences than mTOR inhibition.

steps.what: PIP3 relieves the SIN1 brake and mTORC2 becomes active.
steps.why: Growth-factor-generated PIP3 engages the SIN1 PH domain, releasing its autoinhibition of the complex.
steps.changed: mTORC2 activity rises in response to growth factors — on a seconds timescale.
steps.consequence: Both mTOR complexes are now downstream of PI3K, but they read it differently: mTORC1 through Akt→TSC→Rheb, mTORC2 through this direct lipid relief.
steps.certainty: Medium mechanistic confidence, emerging consensus, one supporting study in this corpus. Drawn as a long dash because it is a compressed relay, not a single event.
steps.matters: This is the cleanest available answer to how growth factors reach mTORC2, and it is weaker evidence than the equivalent step in the mTORC1 arm. Worth noticing: the two complexes are not equally well understood, and the map shows that asymmetry rather than smoothing it over.

steps.what: mTORC2 phosphorylates Akt on S473.
steps.why: This is mTORC2's signature reaction. Akt needs both T308 from PDK1 and S473 from mTORC2 for full activity against many substrates.
steps.changed: Akt becomes fully active — and Akt is what activates mTORC1's upstream arm.
steps.consequence: mTORC2 therefore sits upstream of mTORC1, through Akt. The two complexes are not parallel branches; one feeds the other.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, multiple studies, and the genetic dissection in mice is the strongest evidence in this route: Rictor or mLST8 loss abolishes signalling to Akt while sparing S6K1.
steps.matters: Here is the structural reason the two-complex question matters clinically. Rapamycin hits mTORC1 but not mTORC2 acutely, so it leaves the Akt-activating arm intact — one more reason blocking mTORC1 does not simply shut the pathway down.

steps.what: Disrupting mTORC2 degrades whole-body glucose handling.
steps.why: Less S473 phosphorylation means weaker insulin signalling, which in mice produces measurable glucose intolerance.
steps.changed: An organism-level metabolic phenotype appears, from a change in one complex.
steps.consequence: This is the leading explanation for the dysglycaemia patients experience on chronic rapalogs.
steps.certainty: Mouse data, tier C, medium mechanistic confidence. In humans the relative contributions of mTORC2 loss, S6K1–IRS-1 feedback and direct beta-cell effects are unresolved.
steps.matters: A complex that was invisible because the standard drug did not hit it turns out to explain that drug's most common serious side effect. That is a strong argument for the Atlas's central habit: knowing which arm a claim rests on, and on which species.

steps.what: And chronic rapamycin may reach mTORC2 after all.
steps.why: Prolonged exposure can interfere with mTORC2 assembly in some cell types — slowly, indirectly, and not universally.
steps.changed: The clean separation that made mTORC2 discoverable becomes unreliable over time.
steps.consequence: The textbook line 'rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 but not mTORC2' is a statement about acute treatment being applied to chronic therapy.
steps.certainty: Contested, low mechanistic confidence, a single supporting study. Cell type and duration both change the answer — which is why this arrow is dashed with an amber halo.
steps.matters: The route closes on an irony worth sitting with. Rapamycin insensitivity is the property that revealed mTORC2 existed; that same property may not hold under the conditions in which the drug is actually used. The tool that made the discovery possible may not describe the therapy.

routes.name: Does any of this actually help a patient?

journey.title: Does any of this actually help a patient?
journey.question: Forty years of mechanism is not a treatment. If mTORC1 drives growth and we have drugs that inhibit it, where does that convert into benefit for a person — and where does it conspicuously fail to?

breakthrough.why: There is no breakthrough paper here and claiming one would be dishonest — clinical translation is not a discovery, it is an accumulation. HUD2007 brought the first mTOR inhibitor approval in renal cancer; MOT2008 established everolimus in the same disease; MCC2011 showed sirolimus stabilises lung function in LAM, the cleanest mechanism-to-benefit case in the pathway; LEE2024 is the systematic review that assembles what human rapamycin data actually supports.

journey.evidence: Randomised controlled trials and one systematic review — the only route in this section built primarily on tier A/B human evidence. Note what that buys and what it does not: trials establish that the drug changes an outcome, not that the mechanism drawn upstream is the reason.
journey.unknowns: Which tumours depend on mTOR remains largely unpredictable from genotype. There is no human lifespan data of any kind. And the pattern that rapalogs delay progression without clearly extending overall survival in several indications is unexplained — the feedback loops are the leading suspect.

routes.summary: The only route here where the badges are mostly B. mTOR drugs already work in people - just not yet for the reason this Atlas cares most about.
routes.story: Read this route next to the amino-acid one and the contrast is the point. There, almost every badge is D. Here they are B - randomised human trials, one of them (temsirolimus in renal cancer) on overall survival. The pathway is not unproven in people. Watch the two arrows into LAM, though: everolimus was tested against the kidney lesion in EXIST-2, while the lung disease itself was treated with sirolimus in MILES. They are different drugs and different endpoints, and collapsing them is a common error. What remains unproven is the longevity claim: every arrow on this page ends in a tumour or an immune endpoint, and not one of them ends in lifespan.

steps.what: Lose the TSC brake and mTORC1 runs unopposed.
steps.why: TSC never touches mTORC1 — it acts on Rheb. This arrow is a deliberate two-step compression, drawn as one link so the clinical story reads cleanly.
steps.changed: Without TSC, Rheb stays GTP-loaded and mTORC1 stays on regardless of the cell's actual circumstances.
steps.consequence: Growth signalling becomes constitutive rather than conditional.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, and this is the one place in the whole map where human genetics establishes causality: TSC1/TSC2 loss causes disease in people.
steps.matters: Every other arm of this pathway is inferred from cells and mice. This one is inferred from patients. That difference is why tuberous sclerosis is the setting where mTOR inhibitors work best — the drug is aimed at the actual cause.

steps.what: Constitutive mTORC1 supports tumour growth.
steps.why: Sustained translation of growth and invasion programmes, plus suppressed autophagy, plus the biosynthetic outputs — mTORC1 supplies much of what a proliferating cell needs.
steps.changed: Proliferation and mass increase.
steps.consequence: That makes mTORC1 a drug target. It does not make it the target in every tumour.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence but INDIRECT, and strongly genotype-dependent: a strong dependency in TSC- and PI3K-pathway-mutant contexts, much weaker elsewhere.
steps.matters: The gap between 'mTORC1 supports tumour growth' and 'inhibiting mTORC1 treats this tumour' is where most of the clinical disappointment of the last twenty years lives. Dependency is contextual; the arrow is not.

steps.what: Everolimus inhibits mTORC1 — partially, and via FKBP12.
steps.why: Same allosteric mechanism as rapamycin, with better oral pharmacokinetics. It obstructs the substrate channel rather than occupying the active site.
steps.changed: S6K1 signalling collapses; 4E-BP1 phosphorylation substantially persists.
steps.consequence: The drug delivers partial, asymmetric inhibition to a tumour that may depend on the arm it does not fully block.
steps.certainty: High confidence, and unusually for this map, supported by tier-B human trial evidence across several indications.
steps.matters: Carry the rapamycin route's lesson into the clinic. The incomplete inhibition that is a curiosity in a cell-biology paper is a therapeutic ceiling in a patient — and it is the reason bi-steric and ATP-competitive inhibitors reached trials.

steps.what: In tuberous sclerosis, it works.
steps.why: The disease is caused by loss of the brake this drug substitutes for. Mechanism and treatment are matched.
steps.changed: Tumours shrink, including subependymal giant-cell astrocytoma and renal angiomyolipoma.
steps.consequence: This is the pathway's clearest mechanism-to-benefit case.
steps.certainty: Tier-B trial evidence in humans; human relevance established. Note the honest scope: these are benign tumours and the benefit is control, not cure — treatment interruption is followed by regrowth.
steps.matters: The best result in the whole map comes from the one disease where the causal lesion is known and the drug addresses it directly. That is the template, and the rest of oncology has struggled to reproduce it precisely because the causal lesion is usually not so clean.

steps.what: In renal cancer the link is association, not demonstrated causation.
steps.why: Renal cancers frequently carry lesions that leave mTORC1 active. That is a correlation between genotype and pathway state, not evidence that mTORC1 activation initiates the disease.
steps.changed: Nothing mechanistically. This arrow records a statistical relationship.
steps.consequence: It explains why the tissue responds to rapalogs at all, and why an exceptional responder could be traced to TSC1 loss.
steps.certainty: Typed as ASSOCIATION, directness unresolved, mechanistic confidence low — the lowest-graded link on the route, deliberately. Drawn dotted and thin.
steps.matters: This step exists to be read sceptically. It sits between two well-evidenced clinical steps, and if it were drawn like them a reader would infer a causal chain that the evidence does not support. Grading it honestly is what stops the route from over-claiming.

steps.what: Temsirolimus improved survival in advanced renal cell carcinoma.
steps.why: A randomised trial in poor-prognosis patients — the result that produced the first mTOR inhibitor approval in oncology.
steps.changed: Overall survival improved versus interferon alfa.
steps.consequence: mTOR moved from a laboratory pathway to a licensed drug target.
steps.certainty: Tier-B randomised controlled trial; human relevance established. This is trial evidence: it establishes that the drug changed an outcome, NOT that the mechanism drawn upstream is the reason.
steps.matters: The distinction in that last sentence is the whole point of the route. A positive trial validates a treatment, not a diagram. Everything above this step remains inferred from cells and mice even after the drug is approved.

steps.what: In lymphangioleiomyomatosis, sirolimus stabilised lung function.
steps.why: LAM involves TSC-pathway lesions, so the same mechanistic logic as tuberous sclerosis applies to a progressive lung disease.
steps.changed: FEV1 decline stabilised during treatment in the MILES trial.
steps.consequence: A rare, previously untreatable progressive disease acquired a therapy derived from pathway biology.
steps.certainty: Tier-B trial; human relevance established. Precision matters here: MILES tested SIROLIMUS in the lung disease. EXIST-2 tested everolimus against renal angiomyolipoma, not the lung disease — a distinction routinely blurred, and an external review of this Atlas caught us blurring it.
steps.matters: Arguably the strongest answer to the route's question. Not a cancer, not a lifespan claim — a specific progressive disease where understanding the pathway produced a treatment that changed the disease course. It is also the example most people have never heard of.

steps.what: And in older adults, low-dose everolimus improved vaccine responses.
steps.why: The same drug class used as an immunosuppressant at transplant doses improved influenza vaccine responses when given intermittently at low dose.
steps.changed: Immune function improved rather than degraded — the opposite direction from the drug's classical use.
steps.consequence: It suggests dose and schedule, not the target, determine whether mTOR inhibition suppresses or rejuvenates immunity.
steps.certainty: Tier-B human trials, but typed CONTESTED with medium confidence, because the direction of effect depends on dose and schedule and the finding has not been uniformly replicated at scale.
steps.matters: The route ends where the field currently is. Forty years of mechanism produced clear wins in rare diseases with known causal lesions, partial wins in cancer limited by feedback and incomplete inhibition, and a genuinely open question about whether intermittent low-dose inhibition can improve ageing physiology in people. No human lifespan data exists. That is not a disappointing ending — it is the accurate one, and it is where the next set of trials is aimed.

routes.name: Why does lifting something heavy make a muscle bigger?
routes.territory: Mechanical load → IGF-1/Akt → mTORC1 → translation → hypertrophy

journey.title: Why does lifting something heavy make a muscle bigger?
journey.question: Muscle grows in response to mechanical load, not to a hormone injection. Somewhere a physical force has to become a molecular signal, and then a decision to build. Where does that conversion happen, and how do we know mTORC1 is required rather than merely present?

breakthrough.why: Did the interruption experiment in people. Human volunteers were given rapamycin before resistance exercise, and the contraction-induced rise in muscle protein synthesis was blocked. Almost everything else in this Atlas is inferred from cells or mice; this placed mTORC1 causally inside a human physiological response. BOD2001 had established the pathway's necessity in rodent muscle, but necessity in a person is a different claim.

journey.evidence: A human interventional study for the causal step, rodent genetics and myotube work for the upstream route. This is the only route in the section whose terminal claim carries human-relevance ESTABLISHED rather than plausible — worth noticing, because it is rare here and it is what an interruption experiment buys you.
journey.unknowns: How mechanical force is actually transduced into mTORC1 activation is not settled: load reaches mTORC1 partly independently of IGF-1, and the mechanosensor has not been identified. Whether the same dependence holds in ageing muscle, where anabolic resistance appears, is untested. And mTORC1 activation is necessary but NOT sufficient — constitutive activation alone does not build healthy muscle.

routes.summary: The one route in this section whose final claim was tested by interrupting it in living people. Follow mechanical load to muscle growth, and notice where the evidence stops being inference.
routes.story: The one route in this section whose final claim was tested by interrupting it in living people. Follow mechanical load to muscle growth, and notice where the evidence stops being inference.

steps.what: You lift something heavy, and mTORC1 activity rises in the muscle.
steps.why: Mechanical loading raises mTORC1 signalling in skeletal muscle. Rapamycin given to human volunteers before resistance exercise BLOCKS the contraction-induced rise in muscle protein synthesis — so mTORC1 is not merely present during the response, it is required for it.
steps.changed: A physical force has become a molecular signal. The muscle has committed to building.
steps.consequence: Everything downstream is the pathway you already know, running on a stimulus that is not a hormone.
steps.certainty: The strongest evidence in this entire section: a human interventional study (DRU2009, tier B), supported by rodent genetics (BOD2001) and pharmacology (ZHO2009). Human relevance ESTABLISHED, not plausible.
steps.matters: Pause on what kind of evidence this is. Almost every other step in this Atlas says 'we showed this in cells and infer it in people'. Here someone gave a drug to humans, removed the pathway, and the response disappeared. That is an interruption experiment in a person, and it is worth far more than any amount of correlative human data.

steps.what: Part of the signal does travel the familiar growth-factor route.
steps.why: Loading and IGF-1 signalling overlap: IGF-1 acting through its receptor and PI3K produces myotube hypertrophy, and the same PI3K arm operates during load.
steps.changed: PIP3 accumulates in the membrane.
steps.consequence: Akt can be recruited, exactly as in the growth-factor route.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, but compressed and drawn as a long dash. Cell and myotube evidence (ROM2001, CAN2002).
steps.matters: Only PART of the signal goes this way, and that qualifier matters. Load reaches mTORC1 partly independently of circulating IGF-1, which is why you cannot substitute a growth-factor injection for the mechanical stimulus. The mechanosensor upstream of this has not been identified — the honest gap in an otherwise well-evidenced route.

steps.what: PIP3 recruits Akt to the membrane.
steps.why: Akt binds PIP3 and is then phosphorylated by PDK1 and mTORC2. Recruitment is not activation; both phosphorylations are required.
steps.changed: Akt becomes active at the membrane.
steps.consequence: The brake downstream can now be released.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence; cell-line evidence, human relevance plausible.
steps.matters: The same recruitment-versus-activation distinction that runs through the whole map. In a muscle context it also means mTORC2 function is quietly required for a hypertrophy response — a dependency invisible in most exercise-physiology accounts.

steps.what: Akt inhibits the TSC complex.
steps.why: Phosphorylation of TSC2 inhibits the complex and moves it away from Rheb.
steps.changed: The master brake comes off.
steps.consequence: Rheb stops being switched off.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: Double-negative logic again: the growth signal in muscle works by removing inhibition, not by adding stimulation. This is why the pathway can respond within an hour of a training set — there is nothing to synthesise, only something to stop doing.

steps.what: Rheb accumulates in its GTP-loaded state.
steps.why: TSC2 is the GAP that forces Rheb to hydrolyse GTP. Inhibited GAP, loaded Rheb.
steps.changed: The mTORC1 on-switch moves into position.
steps.consequence: mTORC1 can be activated wherever the two meet.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: Nutrient state still gates this, through location. A trained muscle in a fasted state does not build — which is the mechanistic basis for the entire field of post-exercise nutrition, visible here as the AND gate the nutrient route describes.

steps.what: mTORC1 is switched on.
steps.why: GTP-Rheb allosterically activates the kinase.
steps.changed: mTORC1 begins phosphorylating its substrates.
steps.consequence: The translational machinery is released.
steps.certainty: Structurally resolved, high mechanistic confidence; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: Convergence point again, reached from a third direction — nutrients, hormones, and now mechanical load all terminate here. That is the strongest argument for why this one node is worth understanding properly: everything that decides whether a cell grows has to come through it.

steps.what: mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP1 and releases the cap on translation.
steps.why: Multi-site phosphorylation makes 4E-BP1 let go of eIF4E.
steps.changed: eIF4E is free. A phosphate was added and an inhibitor stopped inhibiting.
steps.consequence: Cap-dependent initiation can proceed.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: This is the arm rapamycin only partly blocks — and yet rapamycin blocked the human hypertrophy response in DRU2009. Worth sitting with: partial inhibition of this step was enough to abolish a whole-body physiological response, which suggests the muscle response has little reserve.

steps.what: eIF4E binds eIF4G and the initiation complex assembles.
steps.why: 4E-BP1 and eIF4G compete for the same surface. Remove one and the other binds.
steps.changed: Ribosomes begin loading onto capped mRNA.
steps.consequence: Protein synthesis rises.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, structurally understood.
steps.matters: Competition rather than catalysis, so the response is stoichiometric and immediately reversible. Muscle expresses its own balance of 4E-BP isoforms, which is one reason the same training stimulus produces different responses in different people and different fibre types.

steps.what: Muscle protein synthesis increases.
steps.why: Cap-dependent initiation rises, selectively favouring a particular class of transcripts rather than everything equally.
steps.changed: The rate and the COMPOSITION of protein synthesis both change.
steps.consequence: Given repeated stimuli and adequate substrate, net protein accretion follows.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence; and this is the exact readout DRU2009 measured in humans and found rapamycin-sensitive.
steps.matters: This is where the human experiment intersects the molecular chain, and it is the reason this route can claim more than the others. The measured variable in the person is the same variable the cell biology predicts.

steps.what: Over days and repeated sessions, the muscle grows.
steps.why: Repeated bouts of elevated synthesis, exceeding breakdown, produce hypertrophy. Raptor-null muscle is dystrophic; rapamycin blocks overload-induced growth.
steps.changed: Fibre cross-sectional area increases.
steps.consequence: The adaptation that the training was for.
steps.certainty: Human relevance established, supported by mouse genetics and human pharmacology. Timescale: days — this is the slowest step in the route by two orders of magnitude.
steps.matters: One honest limit to end on. mTORC1 activation is NECESSARY for healthy hypertrophy but not SUFFICIENT: constitutively activating mTORC1 in muscle does not produce good muscle, it produces inflammation and dysfunction. The signal has to be intermittent. That is a general lesson about this pathway — it is a switch that is meant to be thrown, not held.

routes.name: What happens, and in what order, when you stop eating?
routes.territory: Nutrient withdrawal → AMPK → mTORC1 off → autophagy → lysosomal renewal

journey.title: What happens, and in what order, when you stop eating?
journey.question: Fasting is usually described as a state — fed or fasted. But a cell does not switch states; it runs a sequence, and the parts of that sequence operate on wildly different timescales. Which responses have happened after a few seconds, and which are still hours away?

breakthrough.why: This is an order-of-events question, so no single paper answers it — the sequence had to be assembled from papers about different steps. GWI2008 and EGA2010 supplied the fast arm (AMPK to Raptor, AMPK to ULK1, seconds to minutes). MAR2012 supplied the mTORC1-to-TFEB step that gates the slow arm. SET2012 supplied the return leg, lysosome to nucleus and back. Read together they give a timeline; read separately none of them is about timing at all.

journey.evidence: Direct biochemistry in cells for the ordering, and its timescale grading comes from the curated timescale field on each interaction rather than from any single time-course experiment. The organism-level end of the route rests on rhesus and mouse data (MAT2017, SOL2014) plus one human safety trial (ROM2016).
journey.unknowns: The ORDER here is defensible; the CLOCK is not. This map holds six ordinal timescale buckets, not rate constants, so it can say what has happened by now but never how fast. Human fasting time-courses for these molecular events do not exist in this corpus. And SOL2014 raises the harder question of whether calories or macronutrient ratio is even the right variable.

routes.summary: Not a clock but an ORDER. Set the BY TIME control to seconds, then minutes, then hours, and watch which parts of the response have happened yet. The pathway does not switch state — it unfolds.
routes.story: Not a clock but an ORDER. Set the BY TIME control to seconds, then minutes, then hours, and watch which parts of the response have happened yet. The pathway does not switch state — it unfolds.

steps.what: You stop eating. mTORC1 signalling falls.
steps.why: Two arms detect it at once: the amino-acid sensors stop reporting sufficiency, and AMPK detects the falling energy charge. Neither alone accounts for the drop.
steps.changed: mTORC1 output declines across all of its substrates.
steps.consequence: Everything mTORC1 was suppressing is now released — and that release runs on a slower clock than the suppression did.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence for the direction. Evidence spans mouse, rhesus and one human safety trial (ROM2016), so human relevance is graded plausible.
steps.matters: Set the BY TIME control to seconds and look at the canvas before reading on. Almost nothing downstream has happened yet. That is the point of this route: fasting is not a state the cell enters, it is a sequence the cell runs, and the interesting part is the ordering.

steps.what: Within seconds: AMPK activates.
steps.why: AMP and ADP bind the AMPK gamma subunit directly, activating it allosterically and protecting its activating phosphorylation. No transcription, no translation, no new protein.
steps.changed: An active kinase exists that did not exist a moment ago.
steps.consequence: The fastest arm of the response is now running.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, direct biochemistry; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: Allosteric activation is the fastest control mechanism a cell has, and the pathway spends it on the energy sensor. That is a priority statement: running out of fuel is the emergency that cannot wait for gene expression.

steps.what: Within minutes: AMPK activates the TSC brake.
steps.why: Phosphorylation at sites distinct from Akt's — same substrate, opposite direction.
steps.changed: TSC GAP activity rises and Rheb starts being switched off.
steps.consequence: The mTORC1 on-switch is withdrawn.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, though on a single tier-D study in this corpus.
steps.matters: Notice the timescale step you just took: seconds to minutes. AMPK activation and AMPK's effect on mTORC1 are not simultaneous, and treating them as one event is what makes fasting look like a switch rather than a cascade.

steps.what: mTORC1 goes quiet.
steps.why: No GTP-Rheb, no allosteric activation — regardless of where mTORC1 is sitting.
steps.changed: The kinase stops phosphorylating substrates. Building stops.
steps.consequence: The brakes mTORC1 was applying to recycling now come off, one substrate at a time.
steps.certainty: Structurally resolved, high mechanistic confidence.
steps.matters: Stopping is the easy half. Everything from here is the cell constructing a recovery programme, and each subsequent step is slower than the last — which is why short and long fasts are not the same intervention on a different scale, but different interventions.

steps.what: Minutes: the block on autophagy initiation lifts.
steps.why: mTORC1 had been phosphorylating ULK1 on S757, preventing AMPK from activating it. With mTORC1 quiet, that block is gone.
steps.changed: ULK1 becomes available.
steps.consequence: Availability is not activity. Something still has to switch it on.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, replicated; cell-line evidence.
steps.matters: Release and activation as separate events, on the same protein, from two different kinases. The cell has built an AND gate on autophagy too: it starts only when mTORC1 is off AND AMPK is on, which stops recycling from firing on a brief dip in either signal.

steps.what: And AMPK provides the activating push.
steps.why: AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 at activating sites — the second half of the gate.
steps.changed: ULK1 is now both released and driven.
steps.consequence: Autophagy initiation begins in earnest.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, direct biochemistry, replicated.
steps.matters: One kinase performing both halves of a switch — stopping the expensive programme and starting the recovery programme — is the economy of this design. And ULK1 phosphorylates AMPK back, so the steady state is a set point rather than a command.

steps.what: Autophagy runs. The cell begins digesting its own components.
steps.why: ULK1 nucleates the machinery that captures cargo and delivers it to lysosomes.
steps.changed: Damaged proteins and organelles are broken down; amino acids are regenerated.
steps.consequence: The cell buys both time and materials — and the materials feed the very sensors that started this.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence for initiation. Autophagic FLUX in tissue is genuinely hard to measure, so quantitative in vivo claims are weaker than the mechanism.
steps.matters: This closes a loop the Atlas cannot yet draw: autophagy-derived amino acids re-enter the sensing machinery, so a fasting cell is partly feeding itself. It is declared as an open loop in the model, because no curated edge carries that final step.

steps.what: Also in minutes: TFEB is released from the nucleus's doorstep.
steps.why: mTORC1 had been phosphorylating TFEB on S211, trapping it in the cytosol via 14-3-3. Quiet mTORC1 means TFEB is free to enter the nucleus.
steps.changed: A transcription factor changes compartment — the slow arm has been armed.
steps.consequence: Gene expression is about to change, which takes hours rather than minutes.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence, and substrate-selective: it depends on FLCN/RagC status, so mTORC1 can be active on S6K1 while TFEB escapes.
steps.matters: The timescale changes character here. Everything before this was post-translational and reversible in minutes. From here the cell is rewriting which proteins exist, and that cannot be undone quickly. Switch BY TIME to hours and watch the rest of the route appear.

steps.what: Hours: TFEB transcribes the autophagy programme.
steps.why: Nuclear TFEB switches on autophagy and lysosomal genes as one coordinated module.
steps.changed: The cell now has MORE autophagy machinery, not just active machinery.
steps.consequence: The response becomes sustainable rather than a burst.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence; cell-line evidence, human relevance plausible.
steps.matters: This is the difference between a short fast and a long one, and it is a difference in kind. The first hour reallocates existing machinery. Later hours build more of it. Any claim that a 16-hour and a 48-hour fast do 'the same thing more' is ignoring this step.

steps.what: The lysosomal compartment itself expands.
steps.why: The same TFEB programme drives lysosomal biogenesis — more lysosomes, not just more autophagosomes.
steps.changed: The organelle on which mTORC1 is regulated is being rebuilt.
steps.consequence: The cell is remodelling the platform that controls the signal that started all of this.
steps.certainty: High mechanistic confidence; and SET2012 established the lysosome-to-nucleus circuit this arm belongs to.
steps.matters: This closes a real feedback loop, and the model detects it as one: TFEB to lysosomal biogenesis to lysosome to mTORC1 to TFEB. Fasting does not just lower mTORC1 signalling — it changes the machine that does the signalling. That is why refeeding after a long fast is not simply the reverse of fasting.

steps.what: Over hours: damaged mitochondria are selectively cleared.
steps.why: AMPK promotes mitophagy, the targeted autophagy of mitochondria.
steps.changed: Mitochondrial quality improves rather than merely mitochondrial number falling.
steps.consequence: This is one of the arms through which fasting is proposed to influence ageing.
steps.certainty: Medium mechanistic confidence, indirect, measured largely with reporter mice — so quantitative claims are model-bound. Human relevance plausible at best.
steps.matters: Quality control rather than accounting. A fasting cell is usually a cell with strained mitochondria, so the same signal that stopped growth is the right trigger for repairing the cause. Note the grade drop: from here the evidence weakens as the claims get more interesting.

steps.what: And over a lifetime, restricted animals live longer.
steps.why: Caloric restriction improved health and survival in rhesus monkeys, and macronutrient composition altered lifespan in mice.
steps.changed: Median and in some studies maximum lifespan increase.
steps.consequence: The molecular sequence you just walked is the leading mechanistic account of why.
steps.certainty: Medium mechanistic confidence, INDIRECT, rhesus and mouse. Human relevance UNTESTED — there is no human lifespan data. The two large rhesus studies famously disagreed depending on the control diet, and SOL2014 found macronutrient RATIO mattered more than total calories.
steps.matters: The route asked what happens and in what order. It can answer that with reasonable confidence for the first few hours in a cell, and it cannot answer it at all for a human lifetime. The gap between those two ends of the same arrow is the single most important thing to carry away from this section — and the reason the Atlas grades human relevance separately from mechanism.

routes.name: Where does this pathway stop being known?
routes.territory: The contested, the unresolved and the untested

journey.title: Where does this pathway stop being known?
journey.question: Every pathway diagram looks equally confident everywhere. This one is not, and it records where. So: which parts of mTOR biology are contested between labs, which have a mechanism nobody has resolved, and which have never been tested in a human at all?

breakthrough.why: There is no breakthrough here by construction — this route is about the absence of one. The papers listed are instead the clearest examples of live disagreement: WOL2015 and SAX2015 established Sestrin2 as a leucine sensor, which competes with the LARS model that this map still carries as contested; HOW2017 showed metformin's mTORC1 inhibition is dose-dependent and mechanistically plural, undermining the tidy AMPK story; SAR2006 is the single study behind the contested claim that chronic rapamycin disrupts mTORC2. Each is good work whose conclusion the field has not closed.

journey.evidence: Deliberately the weakest evidence in the Atlas, and the grading is the point: 7 interactions are typed contested, 8 carry low mechanistic confidence, 13 have human relevance untested. Those counts are computed from the model, so this route cannot drift from the data it is complaining about.
journey.unknowns: That is the entire route. But the meta-unknown is worth stating: gaps here are computed against THIS corpus, not against the literature. A gap may mean nobody has done the experiment, or it may mean the Atlas has not yet found the paper — and an external review already caught one case of the second kind. Treat every step as a hypothesis about the evidence, testable by finding the study that closes it.

routes.summary: Every other route shows you what the Atlas holds. This one walks the weakest links on purpose: seven contested interactions, eight with low mechanistic confidence, thirteen with no human evidence at all. Read it as a guide to reading evidence, not as a confession.
routes.story: Every other route shows you what the Atlas holds. This one walks the weakest links on purpose: seven contested interactions, eight with low mechanistic confidence, thirteen with no human evidence at all. Read it as a guide to reading evidence, not as a confession.

steps.what: Two labs proposed two different leucine sensors, and the field has not fully closed the question.
steps.why: Sestrin2 binds leucine with an affinity in the range over which intracellular leucine actually fluctuates. LARS, a leucyl-tRNA synthetase, was independently proposed to moonlight as a leucine sensor acting on the Rag GTPases. Both cannot be the primary sensor in the same cell.
steps.changed: Nothing in the cell. What changes is how much weight you should put on either arrow.
steps.consequence: This map draws both, and marks LARS as contested with a dashed line and an amber halo.
steps.certainty: Contested consensus, LOW mechanistic confidence, human relevance untested. The LARS model has not reproduced cleanly across labs.
steps.matters: Start here because it is the cleanest example of the general problem. A pathway diagram that showed only the winning model would be more comfortable and less true; one that showed both without marking which is disputed would be worse still. The honest option is the one that costs a dashed line and an explanation.

steps.what: The proposed mechanism — LARS acting as a GAP for RagD — is the weakest link in the amino-acid arm.
steps.why: A moonlighting GAP function for a tRNA synthetase is an unusual claim, and the reproduction record is mixed.
steps.changed: Nothing. This is an unresolved mechanism, not an event.
steps.consequence: If it is wrong, the amino-acid arm is simpler than this map suggests. If it is right, there is a second sensing route nobody has integrated.
steps.certainty: Contested, low mechanistic confidence, untested in humans — and the validator flags that no boundary conditions are stated for it, which is itself a curation gap this route is happy to expose.
steps.matters: Notice that the Atlas is admitting a hole in its own curation here rather than hiding it. A validator warning left visible is more useful than a warning silenced.

steps.what: Glutamine may reach mTORC1 without the Rag GTPases at all.
steps.why: A Rag-independent, Arf1-dependent route has been reported. If real, it means the lysosomal recruitment story is not the only way in.
steps.changed: Potentially the architecture of the whole nutrient arm.
steps.consequence: The map draws it dotted and thin, because the claim is large and the reproduction is not uniform.
steps.certainty: Contested, low mechanistic confidence, human relevance untested.
steps.matters: This one matters disproportionately because of what it would overturn. Most contested edges are details; this is a contested claim about whether the central mechanism is complete. Weight of a claim and strength of its evidence are independent, and this step has high weight with low evidence.

steps.what: A step everyone draws confidently has a mechanism nobody has resolved.
steps.why: That GATOR2 inhibits GATOR1 is not in doubt — it is in every textbook figure. HOW it does so catalytically is still argued, even after the GATOR2 structure was determined.
steps.changed: Nothing. This is a hole in the middle of a canonical pathway.
steps.consequence: Every account of amino-acid sensing passes through a step whose mechanism is an open question.
steps.certainty: Consensus graded EMERGING with medium mechanistic confidence — deliberately not established, despite how confidently the step is usually drawn.
steps.matters: This is the most instructive step in the route. It is not contested, not obscure, and not weakly evidenced — it is simply unresolved, in a place where the diagram looks finished. Textbook confidence and mechanistic understanding are different things, and a map that grades them the same teaches the wrong lesson.

steps.what: The most-prescribed drug that touches this pathway has a contested mechanism.
steps.why: Complex I inhibition raising AMP, AMPK-independent Rag inhibition, lysosomal PEN2–ATP6AP1 sensing and gut-microbiome effects have all been proposed. HOW2017 showed the mTORC1 effect is dose-dependent and mechanistically plural.
steps.changed: Nothing mechanistically. What changes is how confidently anyone can say why metformin works.
steps.consequence: Claims that metformin acts 'via AMPK' are shorthand for an unsettled question.
steps.certainty: Contested, LOW mechanistic confidence. And the boundary condition is decisive: concentrations used in cell culture routinely exceed plasma levels achieved at clinical doses.
steps.matters: Dose is the whole argument, and it is the most commonly ignored variable in translating cell biology. A mechanism demonstrated at 5 mM in a dish may be irrelevant at 20 uM in a patient. Any in vitro mechanism claim should come with the concentration attached.

steps.what: So the downstream link inherits the uncertainty.
steps.why: If the route from metformin to AMPK is unsettled, the route from metformin to mTORC1 cannot be firmer than its weakest segment.
steps.changed: Nothing. This is uncertainty propagating along a chain.
steps.consequence: Metformin's mTOR-lowering effect is real and reproducible; its mechanism is not settled, and the two facts are often conflated.
steps.certainty: Contested, low mechanistic confidence, indirect. Cited across mammalian cells and mice.
steps.matters: Uncertainty compounds along a path, and no pathway diagram shows that. If a route has three steps at medium confidence, the endpoint is not medium confidence. The Atlas grades each step but cannot yet grade a PATH — a genuine limitation of this design, worth naming.

steps.what: Whether chronic rapamycin hits mTORC2 rests on a single study in this corpus.
steps.why: Prolonged exposure was reported to disrupt mTORC2 assembly in some cell types. It is not the acute, direct inhibition seen with mTORC1, and it is not universal.
steps.changed: Nothing acutely. Over weeks, possibly a great deal.
steps.consequence: The textbook claim 'rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 but not mTORC2' is a statement about acute treatment being applied to chronic therapy.
steps.certainty: Contested, LOW mechanistic confidence, one supporting study. Cell type and duration both change the answer.
steps.matters: The clinical stakes are inverted relative to the evidence. This is one of the weakest-evidenced edges in the Atlas, and it may explain the most common serious side effect of the drug class. Low confidence does not mean low importance — which is exactly why the two are graded separately.

steps.what: An association presented in a chain of causal claims.
steps.why: Renal cancers frequently carry lesions that leave mTORC1 active. That is a correlation between genotype and pathway state — not evidence that mTORC1 activation initiates the disease.
steps.changed: Nothing mechanistically. This arrow records a statistical relationship.
steps.consequence: It explains why the tissue responds to rapalogs, and why an exceptional responder was traceable to TSC1 loss. It does not establish causation.
steps.certainty: Typed ASSOCIATION, directness UNRESOLVED, mechanistic confidence low — the lowest grade available, applied deliberately.
steps.matters: Correlation sitting between two well-evidenced clinical steps is the most dangerous position on any pathway map, because the reader's eye carries causality across it. Typing it as an association and drawing it dotted is the only defence, and it only works if someone reads the grade.

steps.what: The pathway's most famous claim has no human evidence at all.
steps.why: Lowering mTOR signalling extends lifespan in yeast, worms, flies and mice — reproducibly, multi-site, in genetically heterogeneous strains.
steps.changed: In those organisms, median and sometimes maximum lifespan.
steps.consequence: In humans: unknown. Not disputed, not negative — simply never measured.
steps.certainty: Human relevance UNTESTED. That grade is arithmetic, not pessimism: no human lifespan trial of any mTOR-lowering intervention exists or could have completed.
steps.matters: Thirteen interactions in this map carry human relevance untested, and every longevity edge is one of them. This is the single most important calibration in the Atlas, because it is the claim most likely to be repeated without its qualifier. Robust in four species is a strong result; it is not a human result.

steps.what: The same gap, for the drug specifically.
steps.why: Rapamycin extends mouse lifespan reproducibly, including when started late in life.
steps.changed: Mouse lifespan. Effects are sex- and strain-dependent, and healthspan and lifespan do not always move together.
steps.consequence: It is the strongest pharmacological longevity result in mammals and the basis for current human interest.
steps.certainty: Tier C mouse, medium mechanistic confidence, human relevance untested. LEE2024 systematically reviewed what human rapamycin data actually supports — and lifespan is not among it.
steps.matters: There is a systematic review in this corpus specifically about human rapamycin data, and the honest summary of it is that the human evidence concerns safety and surrogate outcomes, not longevity. When a claim has a systematic review and the review does not support the popular version, the gap is not in the science — it is in the retelling.

steps.what: A case where the direction of effect itself is contested.
steps.why: The same drug class is an immunosuppressant at transplant doses, yet intermittent low-dose everolimus improved influenza vaccine responses in older adults.
steps.changed: Immune function — in opposite directions depending on dose and schedule.
